text.text: How to design a panel study for investigating bivariate dynamics using continuous-time modeling.
Psychological Methods.
When planning a longitudinal panel study, one of the most important decisions is when to collect the data.
Using simulations, we evaluated a continuous-time version of the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model-a statistical model that can handle unequally spaced measurement occasions.

We varied sample size, number of measurement occasions, and the timing of assessments, and then examined how well the model recovered dynamic features (such as temporal stability and cross-effects between the two processes).
Our results indicate that collecting more repeated measurements and using larger samples were the most influential factors for enhancing estimation performance.
Cross-effects between the two processes were notably hard to recover.
They showed low estimation efficiency and low statistical power across many conditions.
Regarding sampling schedules, performance was similar across designs, and prior knowledge of the system dynamics did not lead to better performing schedules.
We introduce the random-within-window and short-and-long-lags designs.
These are simple schedules that include irregular time intervals by design and require no prior knowledge about the bivariate dynamics.
We pro-vide ready-to-use R code for generating them.

We also provide R code to fit continuous-time random-intercept crosslagged panel models to data from any panel study, enabling researchers to take advantage of irregular time intervals rather than treating them as a nuisance.
Finally, we illustrate the methods with data from a panel study on self-esteem and depression.
Together, these resources help researchers design more efficient longitudinal studies and draw more precise conclusions about change over time
Panel studies are common in behavioral sciences, particularly when the focus lies in the examination of the temporal unfolding of at least two processes over the course of time.
Typically, panel data comprise a few measurement occasions or waves (e.g., three to five; Orth et al., 2021), following a sample of participants across a relatively large time span (e.g., 5 years).

text.text: This differs from other types of studies, such as intensive longitudinal designs employing more repeated measurements, fewer participants (even N=1) and a smaller time span.
One of the main goals of panel studies is to examine the time-lagged reciprocal effects between the variables of interest.
In the absence of an experimental design, this is the method by which evidence for reciprocal Granger-causal relationships is gathered (Granger, 1969).
text.formatted: In the absence of an experimental design, this is the method by which evidence for reciprocal Granger-causal relationships is gathered <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Granger, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: Dynamic longitudinal models are often used to analyze panel data for this purpose (Usami et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Dynamic longitudinal models are often used to analyze panel data for this purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Usami et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These models are dynamic in the sense that they describe how the variables evolve over time as a function of their own and each other's previous states.
By far, the most common approach is to specify these models within a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework.
This entails that the data are structured in a wide format, and each column collects a measurement occasion at a specific time, which implies a discrete treatment of time.

That is, discrete-time (DT) models represent change through transitions between successive measurement occasions, such that the modeled effects are tied to the time interval separating those occasions.

Therefore, estimated values for the parameters capturing autoregressive effects (i.e., from previous states of the same process) and cross-lagged effects (i.e., from other processes past states) are dependent on the specific time interval between observations (Voelkle et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Therefore, estimated values for the parameters capturing autoregressive effects (i.e., from previous states of the same process) and cross-lagged effects (i.e., from other processes past states) are dependent on the specific time interval between observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Voelkle et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This leads to a major problem: The magnitude of the time-lagged effects found for the same pair of variables can change greatly between studies with different times between observations (Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Voelkle et al., 2012; Voelkle & Oud, 2013).
text.formatted: This leads to a major problem: The magnitude of the time-lagged effects found for the same pair of variables can change greatly between studies with different times between observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dormann & Griffin, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Voelkle et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Voelkle & Oud, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, in a study where anomia and authoritarianism are measured annually, both processes would appear to be quite stable due to the presence of a high time-lag autoregressive effect.
Meanwhile, if measurements were taken every 6 years, the stability (i.e., autoregressive) effect of both variables would be diminished, even close to zero (Voelkle et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, if measurements were taken every 6 years, the stability (i.e., autoregressive) effect of both variables would be diminished, even close to zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Voelkle et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This phenomenon occurs because the first measurements have a greater capacity to explain subsequent measurements of the same variable when they are closer in time (e.g., after 1 year) compared with those that are more distant in time (e.g., after 5 years), resulting in different parameter values.

The trend is different for cross-lagged effects, as the effect of one process on another typically becomes stronger after a certain amount of time and then diminishes in strength as the time between measurements increases (Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Driver, 2025; Ryan & Hamaker, 2022; Voelkle et al., 2012).

text.text: An increasingly frequent alternative to address the issue of interval-dependent parameters is the use of continuous-time (CT) models (de Haan-Rietdijk et al., 2017; Deboeck & Preacher, 2016; Oud & Jansen, 2000; Ryan et al., 2018; Voelkle et al., 2012; Voelkle & Oud, 2013).

text.text: In this framework, the longitudinal trajectories of the variables are assumed to unfold continuously, and each measurement is considered a discrete realization of this continuous process (Deboeck & Preacher, 2016; Voelkle et al., 2012).

text.text: Given that emotional and behavioral processes are likely to exist and fluctuate between observations, this framework is particularly useful to analyze them.
Dynamical CT models involve working with differential equations, which allow estimating parameters that characterize change for an infinitesimally small time interval.
This entails a very important advantage: The time-dependent parameters can then be rescaled and interpreted for a given time interval of interest.

Another important advantage of CT models is their ability to naturally account for irregular time intervals between observations, both between and within individuals, providing greater flexibility in the measurement of variables (Ryan et al., 2018).

text.text: One critical aspect when designing a longitudinal study is deciding when to measure.

Determining the optimal number and spacing of measurement occasions can be challenging, as researchers often lack enough knowledge about the causal process and the shape of the trajectories (Adolph et al., 2008; Collins & Graham, 2002). Cole and Maxwell (2009) pointed out that measuring with inadequate time intervals can lead to underestimated effect sizes and, therefore, misinterpretations of causal relations.

text.text: According to them, researchers must balance two issues: (a) allowing sufficient time for changes in one variable to influence the other variable while (b) ensuring the effect is measured before it disappears over time.
A few works have addressed this problem in the context of in-tensive longitudinal data (ILD) and ambulatory assessment.
For example, Seizer et al. (2024) provided a comprehensive review and considerations for designing a longitudinal study and its data collection.

text.text: However, they recognized the difficulties in the absence of strong theoretical guidelines for sampling rates and recommend avoiding undersampling and using pilot studies.
The latter recommendation has been made by other authors too (e.g., Adolph et al., 2008; Hopwood et al., 2022).

text.text: The use of continuous-time models does not eliminate the need to make appropriate decisions about when to measure variables.
Recently, Batra et al. (2023) examined the ability of different sampling rates to recover the parameters in univariate autoregressive (AR(1)) models applied to ILD.

text.text: They considered the optimal sampling rate (OSR) to be the one that minimizes the standard error of the model parameters (i.e., optimizes estimation efficiency).

By specifying the CT parameters and the number of repeated measurements, it is possible to calculate the reliability of the estimates using the inverse Fisher information as a function of the sampling rate to obtain the interval that minimizes the standard errors.
Importantly, and in contrast to the existing literature on ILD, few studies have addressed this problem in the context of panel studies.

One exception is the work by Dormann and Griffin (2015), who proposed a set of formulae-both for DT and CT approaches-to calculate the optimal time interval (OTL) given a set of generating parameters.

Despite these previous works, the crucial problem of deciding when to measure is far from resolved, and several important problems remain.

First, most of them focus on intensive longitudinal data, which involves studying processes that evolve rapidly through frequent measures taken in a relatively small number of participants (e.g., positive or negative affect, measured during several days or weeks).

Much less attention has been paid to the adequate design of panel studies, which typically involve studying processes that evolve over longer periods, by taking less repeated measures, over longer time spans, and with larger samples.
Second, and importantly, the literature examining the consequences of the temporal design of measures has focused almost exclusively on discrete time modeling (e.g., Kuiper & Ryan, 2018).
text.formatted: Second, and importantly, the literature examining the consequences of the temporal design of measures has focused almost exclusively on discrete time modeling (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Kuiper & Ryan, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Timmons & Preacher (2015) investigated how the recovery of a non-dynamical (linear and non-linear) univariate process is influenced by the number and spacing of measurements within a fixed study duration.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Timmons & Preacher (2015)</ref> investigated how the recovery of a non-dynamical (linear and non-linear) univariate process is influenced by the number and spacing of measurements within a fixed study duration.

text.text: Non-linear processes were found to be especially sensitive to both the number of observations and their distribution over time, as well as the interaction between them.
For these non-linear trajectories, the main piece of advice derived from these results was to accumulate most of the measurements around the moment of greatest curvature of the trajectory.
However, their study did not delve into trajectories with no specific curvature, such as processes that follow stable trajectories that fluctuate around a mean level.
Furthermore, these recommendations stem from studying deterministic processes and it is, therefore, unclear the extent to which they can be extended to stochastic systems.
A stochastic system is one in which the variable of interest cannot be fully predicted based on its state at previous points in time.
The source of this uncertainty is usually conceptualized as dynamic or innovative shocks to the trajectories.
Generally, the variability of these innovations is modeled as a variance parameter, sometimes called dynamic error (Cáncer & Estrada, 2023; Schuurman et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Generally, the variability of these innovations is modeled as a variance parameter, sometimes called dynamic error <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cáncer & Estrada, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Schuurman et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This dynamic error has a crucial role in longitudinal processes, because their stability over time depends on both these dynamics shocks and the value of the autoregressive and cross-lagged parameters (i.e., given a fixed value for a process' autoregression parameter, the observed autocorrelation between repeated measures will be lower with a higher variance of the stochastic innovations; see the next section for more details).
Designing a panel study (and longitudinal studies in general) requires decisions about the time interval between measures and the total number of measurements.
These aspects have received considerable attention in the methodological literature.
However, the overall duration of the study and the distribution of measurements throughout are equally critical design choices, yet they remain relatively underexplored.
For instance, in a hypothetical research project spanning a 5-year period, if new waves of measurement were taken, for example, every 6 months, the study would include up to 10 repeated measurements.

However, if there were funding for, say, only six waves of data collection, the researchers would need to decide to either take them every 10 months and cover the whole time range, or take them every 6 months instead (i.e., for theoretical reasons) and cover only a fraction of the total available time range.
Furthermore, measurement occasions do not need to be evenly spaced.

For example, they can be randomly distributed throughout the study, resulting in varying time intervals both between and within participants, while maintaining a constant average interval overall (e.g., Hasl et al., 2024; Real-Brioso et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, they can be randomly distributed throughout the study, resulting in varying time intervals both between and within participants, while maintaining a constant average interval overall (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hasl et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Real-Brioso et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Measurements can also be concentrated within a specific phase of the study (e.g., at the beginning or when greater curvature of the trajectories is expected).

Considering this, the term sampling rate, often used in the literature, may be too narrow, and researchers should focus on the sampling schedule instead, as it encompasses all the aspects related to the timing of data collection.
Noteworthy, it is highly problematic to accommodate irregular measurement occasions with DT dynamical models, as they assume fixed and evenly spaced intervals.
This constraint limits design flexibility and often forces researchers to impose regularity on data col-lection schedules.
In contrast, CT models inherently account for variability in time intervals because the exact timing of each measurement is explicitly incorporated into the model (Ryan et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In contrast, CT models inherently account for variability in time intervals because the exact timing of each measurement is explicitly incorporated into the model <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ryan et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This feature enables more flexible study designs, such as irregular or strategically concentrated measurement schedules.
In other words, by adopting CT models, researchers can access a wider range of strategies for designing panel studies.
These extended design possibilities have received little attention to date. Hasl et al. (2024) delved in how the variability in measurement intervals affects parameter recovery in a single process.
text.formatted: These extended design possibilities have received little attention to date. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hasl et al. (2024)</ref> delved in how the variability in measurement intervals affects parameter recovery in a single process.

text.text: However, the performance of CT models that simultaneously incorporate two interrelated processes in panel data has not been evaluated.

This is an important issue, as the interpretation of cross-effects, which is usually the central focus of bivariate longitudinal studies, is sensitive to many methodological decisions regarding data modeling (see Driver, 2025).
text.formatted: This is an important issue, as the interpretation of cross-effects, which is usually the central focus of bivariate longitudinal studies, is sensitive to many methodological decisions regarding data modeling (see <ref type="bibr">Driver, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, no work has conducted a systematic evaluation of how the degree of stochasticity could change sampling needs in panel studies.

Therefore, this paper seeks to address these gaps by comprehensively examining the capacity of continuous-time models to identify and estimate parameters governing the causal relations between two interrelated processes in panel data.
We focus on one of the most common statistical models in this context: the Random-Intercept Cross Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM), which we explain in the next section.

The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) was proposed as an extension of the Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CLPM), and developed to account for different sources of stability in psychological constructs (Berry & Willoughby, 2017; Hamaker et al., 2015; Zyphur et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) was proposed as an extension of the Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CLPM), and developed to account for different sources of stability in psychological constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Berry & Willoughby, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hamaker et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zyphur et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the CLPM, which only models stability through autoregressive relations, RI-CLPM separates within-person (statelevel) fluctuations from stable between-person (trait-level) differences.

This distinction is very useful, as failing to account for stable inter-individual differences leads to misinterpretations of causality and inflated intra-individual parameter estimates (Hamaker et al., 2015; Lucas, 2023; Mulder & Hamaker, 2021).
text.formatted: This distinction is very useful, as failing to account for stable inter-individual differences leads to misinterpretations of causality and inflated intra-individual parameter estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hamaker et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucas, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Mulder & Hamaker, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The RI-CLPM has been widely applied in contexts where psychological processes can be assumed to involve two distinct components: a stable, trait-like component that reflects consistent individual differences over time, and a more transient, state-like component that captures short-term variations influenced by prior states (Mulder & Hamaker, 2021; Orth et al., 2021 Orth et al., , 2024;; Usami et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The RI-CLPM has been widely applied in contexts where psychological processes can be assumed to involve two distinct components: a stable, trait-like component that reflects consistent individual differences over time, and a more transient, state-like component that captures short-term variations influenced by prior states <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Mulder & Hamaker, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Orth et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orth et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Usami et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A common example is the trait-state distinction in depression (see Endler et al., 2000; Schrader, 1994): individuals differ in their general level of depressive symptoms (trait level), but also experience short-term variations (state level), with levels changing and carrying over from one week to the next.

text.text: Although we will use a continuous-time implementation of the RI-CLPM, we start by describing the discrete-time form, since it is much more common in the literature.

In the usual discrete-time specification of the RI-CLPM (Equations 1 and 2), the observed variables xi and yi are explained (i.e., regressed on) three components: 1) the so-called "grand means" (μx,t and μy,t), which are time-varying group means, 2) the random-intercepts (RIx and RIy), which are the time-invariant stable trait factors that represent an individual's trait-like deviations from the grand means (i.e., stable between-individual differences) and 3) x * i,t and y * i,t , which are the temporal deviations from the expected scores of individual i at occasion t: 𝑥 𝑖,𝑡 = 𝜇 𝑥,𝑡 + 𝑅𝐼 𝑥,𝑖 + 𝑥 * 𝑖,𝑡 [2]

The temporal deviations in the latter term of each equation are, in turn, modeled as a function of three components: 𝑥 * 𝑖,𝑡 = 𝑎 11 • 𝑥 * 𝑖,𝑡-1 + 𝑐 12 • 𝑦 * 𝑖,𝑡-1 + 𝑑𝑥 𝑖,𝑡 [3] 𝑦 * 𝑖,𝑡 = 𝑎 22 • 𝑦 * 𝑖,𝑡-1 + 𝑐 21 • 𝑥 * 𝑖,𝑡-1 + 𝑑𝑦 𝑖,𝑡 [4]
The first term in Equations 3 and 4 captures the influence of the deviation at the previous time point (t-1) in the same variable, through the autoregressive effects (AR, a11 and a22).
They represent the amount of 'within-person carry-over effect' (Hamaker, 2015).
text.formatted: They represent the amount of 'within-person carry-over effect' <ref type="bibr">(Hamaker, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, if a11 is positive, individuals with scores in x above their expected level at time t-1 will likely have scores above their expected level at the next time t.
The second term captures the influence of the deviation at t-1 on the other variable, or the cross-lagged effects (CL, c12 and c21).

They capture the extent to which the level in one process can be predicted from earlier deviations from the expected level in the other variable, after accounting for both the process's own previous deviation and its overall structural change.
For example, if c12 is negative, individuals that scored less than usual in one process (yt-1) will tend to have higher at the next occasion in the other process (xt).
Finally, the residual components (dxi,t and dyi,t) characterize the innovations or dynamic errors.
These components can be interpreted as random alterations that affect, at a latent level, the fluctuations of the processes.
Importantly, their effects are carried over subsequent times (Cáncer & Estrada, 2023; Schuurman et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Importantly, their effects are carried over subsequent times <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cáncer & Estrada, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Schuurman et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, a random event such an unexpected stressful situation (e.g., a sudden dismissal) may affect the latent level of depressive symptoms, and may consequently affect the following days or weeks.

Thes magnitude and number of these random impacts are captured by the innovation or dynamic error variance of each process, which is often assumed to be time-invariant σdx 2 and σdy 2 , and can be correlated (σdxy 2 ).
This is a stationary structural equation model, meaning that all the parameters have constant value over time.
Therefore, the dynamic parameters (including the two AR and the two CL) have the same value for any given pair of observations t-1 and t.
Furthermore, the intervals between observations are assumed to remain constant over time.
Note that Equations 3 and 4 are often included in a single matrix equation.
Here we present them separately for ease of understanding.
The following section presents the corresponding continuous-time state-space matrix formulation.
In this study, we illustrate how to estimate the RI-CLPM described above in continuous-time (CT).
This has several benefits.

In contrast with the better-known specification in discrete time, typically estimated within a structural equation modeling framework (e.g., Mulder & and Hamaker, 2021), CT modeling allows flexibly incorporating heterogeneous time intervals between measurement occasions, both across and within participants.
text.formatted: In contrast with the better-known specification in discrete time, typically estimated within a structural equation modeling framework (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Mulder & and Hamaker, 2021)</ref>, CT modeling allows flexibly incorporating heterogeneous time intervals between measurement occasions, both across and within participants.

text.text: This is advantageous in most longitudinal studies, and particularly in panel studies, for several reasons: a) Even when a research design schedules all participants to be measured at the same time points (i.e., waves), logistical constraints and unforeseen circumstances often make it impossible to collect data from everyone at the same time.

b) Some degree of data incompleteness is almost inevitable, which results in uneven time intervals between observations. c) Parameter estimates in CT models are independent of the time interval between measurements.
Therefore, they can be rescaled to any time interval of interest, which allows for greater comparability across studies (Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Voelkle et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Therefore, they can be rescaled to any time interval of interest, which allows for greater comparability across studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dormann & Griffin, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Voelkle et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: d) CT models make it possible to move beyond evenly spaced waves and implement more flexible sampling schedules.
For example, oversampling during specific periods of interest or introducing variability in time intervals both between and within individuals.
The present work leverages CT modeling to introduce and assess the performance of several such flexible sampling schedules for panel data.
Various modeling frameworks are available for estimating dynamic models with latent variables in CT.
Here, we will specify a continuous-time RI-CLPM (CT-RI-CLPM) as a state-space model (SSM; Chow et al., 2010; Hunter, 2018).

text.text: An SSM is composed of two equations: the state equation (Equation 5), which represents the dynamics of change in the latent variables, and the output equation (Equation 6), which links latent variables to observed measures:

text.text: In equation 5, f(t) is a vector including all the latent variables (in this framework, they are termed latent states) at time t, and A is the drift matrix of continuous-time autoregressive and cross effects, which determines how the latent states change over an infinitesimally small time interval.

The term But represents the influence of observed exogenous covariates u(t), whose effect is captured by the loading matrix B. In addition, q(t) accounts for stochastic disturbances, often referred to as dynamic errors or process noise (i.e. innovations).
These disturbances are typically drawn from a normal distribution, with mean zero and variance to be estimated.
That is, the greater the variance of the dynamic errors, the less stable the process will be, because the state of the system at time (t) will be less predictive of its change.
The output equation (Eq. 6) is very similar to the measurement model of a discrete-time SEM.
Vector mt includes the observed variables at time t.
Matrix C contains the measurement structure, i.e., the factor loadings linking the latent states to time-specific observed variables.
The term Dut represents the direct effects of covariates on observed measures, and r(t) captures measurement errors.

When specifying a bivariate RI-CLPM in a continuous-time SSM, the latent structure includes two components: (1) the time-varying states for each variable and (2) the random intercepts (RI), which capture the stable, time-invariant individual differences with their variances.
The latent state vector f(t) must be therefore expanded to accommodate these two latent variables for each process.

Note that, in this specification, we do not include any additional covariates, and thus the matrices B, Das well as the measurement error variances and covariance-are fixed to zero and can be removed from the equations.

This study aims to examine the influence of various design choices on the recovery of the temporal dynamics between two processes in panel studies with continuous-time (CT) modeling.

In particular, we evaluated the performance of a CT implementation of the Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model, with special interest in the recovery of the parameters that characterize auto-and cross-effects.
We tested various patterns of relationship, including strong, weak, and asymmetrical dynamic influences between the two processes.
We also varied the ratio of within-vs. between-individual variance, thereby assessing the effects of different degrees of stochasticity (i.e., the magnitude of the random innovations).
This is a novel and important contribution to literature, since stochasticity is key to understanding the stability of psychological processes.
Simultaneously, we evaluated the impact of key aspects of the study design: sample size, number of repeated measures, sampling schedule, and total duration of the study.

Regarding the sampling schedule, we examined whether the sampling methods that have been proposed for longitudinal studies to determine the optimal measurement interval (i.e., Adolf et al., 2021; Dormann & Griffin, 2015) lead to adequate parameter estimation in panel studies under the different sets of population parameters.

text.text: We will compare such methods with a novel approach introduced in this work: the short and long lags designs.
Finally, we illustrated an empirical application of the CT-RI-CLPM, to demonstrate their practical implications in real-world data.
We expected to find an interaction between the number of repeated measurements, the sampling plan, and the intervals between assessments.

Specifically, we expected that conditions with a greater number of measurements would show better parameter recovery, and this positive effect would be larger when observations are more closely spaced.

Regarding the population generating parameters, we varied 1) the values of the drift A matrix to represent distinct dynamic patterns (i.e., both cross-effect strong, both weak, or one strong and one weak, i.e., unidirectional); and 2) the ratios of within-and between-individual variance, thereby modeling different levels of stochasticity by shifting variance toward the within-person level.
Each of these conditions was examined under a set of distinct sampling schedules and sample sizes.

text.text: The primary goal of this study was to evaluate how key design choices influence the recovery of temporal dynamics between two processes in panel studies, and to Our results indicate that the sample size and the number of repeated measurements had the strongest impact on parameter recovery, whereas differences attributable to sampling schedules were comparatively minor.
In general, estimation was adequate in conditions with a large volume of information: 12 measurement occasions, and a sample of 2000 cases.

When substantial cross-effects are expected, these requirements can be relaxed, with adequate recovery achievable using more conventional sample sizes (from 250 cases) and fewer measurement occasions (six per case).
The greatest estimation challenges were found with auto-and cross-effect parameters (a11, a22, c12 and c21) in the drift matrix.
This was especially pronounced for cross-effects, which are often the primary focus in applications of cross-lagged modeling.
Our findings indicate that cross-effect point estimates are generally unbiased, but estimation efficiency is low, resulting in wide sampling distributions.
For strong cross-effects, statistical power was adequate with samples of 250 cases or more.
However, adequate inferential decisions about weak cross-effects required substantially larger samples (at least 2000 cases) combined with 12 or more measurement occasions.

Some systematic bias was observed under conditions with asymmetric drift and diffusion matrices: in these scenarios, one process exhibited higher stochasticity, which partially obscured the influence of the other process, pulling the corresponding crosseffect estimate toward zero.

This bias was small in absolute terms but became apparent when computing relative bias due to the small magnitude of the true values, and was effectively mitigated by increasing the number of measurement occasions.
Parameters related to between-person components and dynamic error (i.e., stochastic innovations) were consistently well recovered across varying rations of within-and between-individual variance.

This suggests that the degree of stochasticity in the process has limited impact on the estimation of the drift and diffusion matrices, whereas factors such as the number of repeated measurements and sample size have a greater influence on accurate recovery, especially of the cross-effects.
In addition, we illustrated the application of a continuous-time RI-CLPM using an empirical dataset.

By estimating the parameters in continuous time and subsequently rescaling them to discrete time, we were able to replicate the findings of the original study, which applied a discrete-time structural equation model to the same data.
The results indicated that depression exerted a greater influence on low self-esteem, consistent with the scar model (Lewinsohn et al., 1981; Orth & Robins, 2013).

text.text: A central implication of our findings concerns how researchers conceptualize the temporal design of longitudinal studies.
Previous literature has focused on identifying an optimal sampling rate, that is, a single ideal time interval between consecutive measurements (Adolf et al., 2021; Dormann & Griffin, 2015).
text.formatted: Previous literature has focused on identifying an optimal sampling rate, that is, a single ideal time interval between consecutive measurements <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adolf et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Dormann & Griffin, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that a more productive framework is to think in terms of a sampling schedule.
This concept encompasses also the total duration of the study and the temporal distribution of measurement occasions, which can be irregular by design.

This shift is enabled by Our findings also challenge the common recommendation to measure as frequently as possible (Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Hopwood et al., 2022; Ram et al., 2017; Seizer et al., 2024).

text.text: The SHALL schedules tested this recommendation directly: they concentrated all but one measurement occasion at the beginning of the study, with only the final occasion placed at the end, effectively maximizing measurement density over a short window.
These schedules obtained the worst results.
In contrast, the remaining sampling schedules distributed occasions across a broader range of time intervals and performed consistently better.
This pattern suggests that in a continuoustime framework, capturing variability across diverse time lags is more informative than concentrating measurements within a too narrow temporal window.

Although satisfactory conditions for recovering the dynamics of a bivariate system were identified, the drift matrix consistently showed lower estimation efficiency than other model components (i.e., greater variability in the sampling distributions of its parameter estimates).
This was especially pronounced for cross-effects, and is consistent with some findings from studies examining intensive longitudinal designs (de Haan-Rietdijk et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This was especially pronounced for cross-effects, and is consistent with some findings from studies examining intensive longitudinal designs (de <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Haan-Rietdijk et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Some empirically plausible conditions, particularly those involving weak cross-effects, led to markedly deficient parameter estimation when design conditions were insufficient.

Furthermore, under conditions with asymmetric drift and diffusion matrices, a subtle but systematic pattern emerged: the cross-effect corresponding to the process with higher stochasticity (c12) was pulled toward zero, accompanied by a slight redistribution of residual variances between the two processes.

This suggests that when the two processes differ substantially in their within-person variability, the elevated noise in one process can partially obscure the influence of the other, leading the model to compensate through small systematic shifts in related parameters.

Although this bias was small in absolute terms (and negligible once a sufficient number of measurement occasions was incorporated), it became apparent in relative bias indices due to division by small true values.
This illustrates a broader point: global indices such as total relative bias can conceal important estimation challenges specific to individual parameters.
More generally, the common practice of evaluating estimation performance through overall bias indices such as RMSRB can be misleading in the context of bivariate dynamic models.
In our study, such indices would suggest that estimation was generally satisfactory, obscuring the severe challenges associated with recovering crosseffects.

Metrics such as robustness to type S error (the rate at which point estimates recover the correct sign) and statistical power (the rate at which the 95% confidence interval falls entirely within the correct sign) proved far more informative.

Both are direct consequences of estimation inefficiency, are easier to interpret, and better capture conditions under which researchers risk drawing substantively incorrect conclusions about directional effects.
We recommend that future simulation studies of bivariate dynamic models adopt these indicators alongside conventional bias metrics.
Finally, our findings should be interpreted in light of the population-generating values used to define simulation conditions.
The classification of cross-effects as "weak" or "strong" depends on factors that warrant further systematic investigation.

Orth et al. (2024) proposed that a discrete-time cross-lagged effect of 0.07 represents a moderate value, but this guideline did not account for the nonlinear dependence of cross-lagged effects on the measurement interval.

We derived our simulation values from studies employing annual measurements, where a "strong" discrete-time crosslagged effect (the third quartile in Orth et al.'s distribution) was approximately 0.08.

This choice, combined with the fact that many panel studies have not reported the time intervals used (Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Miller et al., 2025), may have restricted the range of continuous-time cross-effect values examined.

text.text: We therefore recommend that researchers carefully consider whether the cross-effects of interest in their substantive domain are likely to be weak or strong, in order to select the appropriate design guidelines from those presented here.
Several issues were unexplored in the present study and therefore remain to be addressed.
First, we have assumed processes that do not present measurement error.

Although estimating a simpler model is a first step in exploring these sampling conditions, previous studies have argued that not including measurement error can affect the estimation of other parameters (Driver, 2024).

Recently, the role of the correlation of the latter in CT models and how it affects cross-effects estimation has been addressed (Kuiper & Hamaker, 2025).

text.text: Therefore, the potential interplay between varying degrees of residual correlation and the estimation of cross-lagged parameters should be further examined to identify possible systematic biases resulting from asymmetric yet differently correlated systems.

Another limitation of the present study is that we have assumed that both processes maintain the same dynamics regardless of whether they are measured at intervals of, for example, two months or one year.
This assumption may not be held in all scenarios.
For example, measuring emotionality on a weekly basis would provide information about individuals' sensitivity and self-regulation in response to minor changes (e.g., everyday unforeseen events).

Instead, if emotionality is measured annually, even with the same instrument, we might obtain information about different processes governing individuals' regulation, e.g., resilience in the face of drastic changes that can occur in life (e.g., relocations, layoffs or the dissolution of a romantic partnership).
This would lead to differences in the dynamic parameters that are not due to mere differences in time interval.
We emphasize the importance of the theoretical foundations in an empirical setting to ensure that, despite using largely unequal time intervals, the same processes are being measured.

On this regard, Andresen et al. (2025) have recently developed an approach that integrates IDL and panel data, enabling different timescales at micro, meso, and macro levels from a discrete-time framework.

text.text: The scope of this study was intentionally restricted to bivariate systems.

An important direction for future research is the extension to trivariate or higher-order systems, which likely face greater estimation challenges given the increased number of parameters in the drift matrix.

Such an extension also raises interpretive complexities: in multivariate systems involving three or more processes, true discrete-time cross-lagged effects may change sign depending on the length of the time interval, a consequence of the matrix exponential that maps the continuous-time drift matrix to its discrete-time counterpart (Voelkle, 2012).

text.text: This complicates the interpretability of the continuous-time sign and represents a substantive challenge that warrants dedicated investigation.

Finally, future work should investigate whether the low estimation efficiency for the dynamic parameters in the drift matrix A, and subsequent low statistical power for the cross-effects, can be alleviated through alternative estimation procedures and/or parameterizations (e.g., Bayesian estimation, penalized likelihood, or previous rescaling of the variables' metrics).

It would be advantageous to conduct bootstrap studies based on single samples for estimating the sampling distributions for the drift matrix parameters and obtaining a clearer picture about the center and dispersion of such distributions (Kulesa et al., 2015).

text.text: This study advances the methodological toolkit for longitudinal research by Based on our findings, we offer the following recommendations for applied researchers using continuous-time models with panel data.
When the magnitude of cross-effects is unknown, relatively large sample sizes are required to ensure accurate estimation, particularly for inferential purposes.
We recommend N ≥ 2000 participants combined with at least ten measurement occasions per case.
Although such sample sizes may seem demanding, they are not uncommon in panel research (M = 1296.4, SD = 2,432.0, Mdn = 493.5 in the systematic review by Orth et al., 2024).

text.text: When prior evidence suggests the presence of strong cross-effects between the processes of interest, smaller samples may suffice.
Specifically, samples of 250-500 participants, measured on six or more times, can adequately detect these effects and identify the dominant process.
The specific distribution of measurement occasions appears to have limited 5.
Caution is warranted when interpreting parameters in the drift matrix, particularly cross-effects, as they exhibit very low estimation efficiency and statistical power.
Researchers should consider whether their expected effect sizes are weak or strong and select their design accordingly.
We hope these empirically grounded tools and recommendations will inform both the design and analysis of future panel studies.

To this end, we conducted a Monte Carlo simulation and assessed the performance of a continuous-time implementation of the Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CT-RI-CLPM) under varying population and design conditions.
Specifically, we manipulated sample size, number of repeated measurements, and sampling schedule, while considering different patterns of dynamic relationships and degrees of stochasticity.

continuous-time modeling, which treats unequal spacing not as a nuisance but as a source of information.Within this framework, we introduced two types of sampling schedules that incorporate unequal time intervals as a deliberate design feature: Random-Within-Window (RWW), with occasions randomly placed within predefined windows of equal average spacing, and Short-and-Long Lags (SHALL-P), with progressively increasing intervals.
Both performed well across conditions.

Notably, previously proposed methods for determining an optimal measurement interval (optimal sampling rate, OSR,Adolf et al., 2021; optimal time lag, OTL, Dormann & Griffin, 2015)  also yielded adequate performance, but did not outperform RWW or SHALL-P, and carry the important disadvantage of requiring prior knowledge of the bivariate dynamics, which is rarely available in practice.

For instance, with 8 measurement occasions and N = 2000, the average standard deviation of the mean standard error of c21 across sampling schedules was only 0.086 across the fifteen populations, indicating negligible differences between schedules.
systematically evaluating the performance of the continuous-time Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CT-RI-CLPM) in panel study contexts.
Although CT modeling has gained traction in ILD settings, its application to panel data remains underexplored.

Our Monte Carlo simulation addresses this gap, and our findings converge on a clear message: sample size and the number of measurement occasions matter far more than the specific temporal placement of those occasions.

A key advantage of continuous-time modeling is that panel studies need not rely on equally spaced waves and can incorporate variability in time lags both between and within individuals, opening new possibilities for study design beyond traditional rigid schedules.

Both are simpler to implement than previously proposed alternatives such as OTL and OSR schedules, and critically, they require no prior information about the population dynamics.
We provide an R function to compute SHALL-P schedules at https://osf.io/vudta.
Researchers should take advantage of the flexibility of continuous-time and statespace models for analyzing panel data with irregular time intervals.
We provided open-source R code for implementing continuous-time RI-CLPMs in OpenMx, thereby lowering the barrier to entry for researchers interested in applying continuous-time methods to panel data.
